title: Lantern and Ledger
premise: In the port city of Vessany, on the eve of revolution, Wendell Almeida works in her father's print shop cutting type and keeping her head down—until a stranger leaves an infant at their door with a note: forget this face. The child, it turns out, is the illegitimate heir of a murdered minister whose papers were never published, and both royalists and republicans will kill to control his story. Wendell secretly prints the minister's suppressed testimony while hiding the boy among the type cases, learning that invisibility is a kind of complicity. In the end she chooses truth over safety: the testimony runs on the day the old regime falls, her father dies shielding the press, and Wendell escapes to exile with the child—not as a bystander to history, but as one of its authors.
about_author: Jude Montrose is the pen name of a former letterpress compositor who spent a decade restoring nineteenth-century printing equipment before turning to fiction. They write historical novels about the people who made records—and the people who tried to erase them.

chapters.title: The Weight of Lead
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Establishes the Almeida print shop, her father's failing eyesight, and her skill as a typeface cutter. She prides herself on being unnoticed by soldiers and censors alike. Emotional beat: quiet pride in smallness, foreshadowing its cost.

chapters.title: A Bundle at the Door
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A rain-soaked stranger leaves an infant with a note reading 'forget this face' and a sealed packet of documents. Her father insists they turn it over to authorities; Wendell hesitates. Emotional beat: fear cracking into reluctant protectiveness.

chapters.title: The Minister's Hand
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, with a flashback fragment. Reading the sealed papers, she recognizes the handwriting of Minister Corvel, rumored assassinated weeks ago—the documents are his testament naming powerful men in both factions. Emotional beat: dawning vertigo as history arrives on her workbench.

chapters.title: Censor's Visit
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A government censor inspects the shop; her father performs loyalty while Wendell hides the baby in the type loft. The censor notices nothing but leaves a list of banned words. Emotional beat: terror sharpening into defiance.

chapters.title: What the Compositor Saw
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Tomas, the shop's journeyman printer, who has guessed about the child and demands answers—or payment for silence. Wendell must decide whether to trust him. Emotional beat: betrayal's possibility versus loneliness of secrets.

chapters.title: The Widow Corvel
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A woman claiming to be the minister's widow comes asking after 'a delivery.' Wendell lies badly. The woman leaves a coin and a threat. Emotional beat: guilt and the first sense of being hunted.

chapters.title: Setting the Forbidden Type
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. He agrees to help print excerpts anonymously if Wendell shares credit and risk. Night work by lamplight; the physical craft of setting dangerous words. Emotional beat: conspiratorial intimacy, the press becoming a weapon.

chapters.title: Republic of Rumor
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Street unrest grows; bread riots; a friend from the market district disappears. Wendell realizes the city is choosing its stories already, and whoever prints first writes history. Emotional beat: urgency replacing caution.

chapters.title: The Face She Cannot Forget
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Quiet interlude: the baby's first word, her father teaching him letters with movable type. She admits she loves him and that love has made her visible. Emotional beat: tenderness shadowed by dread.

chapters.title: Betrayal Priced in Bread
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. A royalist agent offers Tomas immunity and money for the documents. He neither accepts nor refuses, and the chapter ends with him pocketing the card. Emotional beat: temptation and self-loathing.

chapters.title: Fire in the Paper District
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Rival printers' shops burn; the censorship bureau escalates. Father Almeida moves the testament pages into hollowed type cases. Emotional beat: siege mentality, the shop as fortress.

chapters.title: The Widow Returns
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The 'widow' returns, reveals she is Corvel's daughter, not his wife, and begs Wendell to publish—but warns that the republican committee wants the testament altered to implicate only royalists. Emotional beat: truth itself becomes contested territory.

chapters.title: Committee of Public Records
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Revolutionary officials summon Tomas and offer the shop a contract: print the official history, sanitized. Refusal means suspicion. Emotional beat: power's velvet threat.

chapters.title: Altered Proofs
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She discovers someone has reset passages of the testament to shift blame—Tomas's composition, under orders. Confrontation in the composing room. Emotional beat: heartbreak; loyalty and truth pull apart.

chapters.title: The Confession of Tomas Ferro
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. He confesses he was the stranger who left the baby—he was Corvel's clerk and could not destroy the heir or the papers. His silence was bought with fear. Emotional beat: shame transmuted into resolve.

chapters.title: Night Run
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Smuggling the plates and the child across the city to a sympathetic underground press; checkpoints, a near-discovery, help from the market women. Emotional beat: solidarity of the invisible.

chapters.title: The Victor's Historian
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The committee's historian visits, offering Wendell a place in the new order if the original testament is surrendered. He speaks gently of necessity. Emotional beat: seduction of legitimacy; she nearly wavers.

chapters.title: What Is Written Cannot Be Unwritten
chapters.summary: Father Almeida's POV. The old man locks himself in the shop overnight and sets the full, unaltered testament in type, knowing what it will cost. Emotional beat: a craftsman's final act of faith in the record.

chapters.title: The Presses at Dawn
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. Soldiers raid the shop as the first sheets come off the press; Father Almeida refuses to surrender the forme and is killed; Tomas holds the door; Wendell escapes with the child and a proof copy through the paper district fires. Emotional beat: climax—grief, fury, and terrible clarity.

chapters.title: Eve of the Fall
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The testament circulates hand to hand overnight; the palace guard wavers as the truth outruns the official story. Wendell watches the city turn from a rooftop, holding the sleeping child. Emotional beat: exhausted awe—history happening to her, because of her.

chapters.title: Ledger Closed
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The new government offers honors and asks her to print their version now. She declines, buries her father beside the river, and burns the committee's flattering contract. Emotional beat: mourning braided with refusal; power corrupts every victor.

chapters.title: Lantern
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, years later, in exile. She runs a small press in a foreign port town; the boy sets his first line of type—a sentence from his father's testament. She lights the shop lantern for the night shift. Emotional beat: resolution—truth outlives regimes, carried hand to hand like flame.
